clinicalPearls: Obesity is defined as a state of excess adipose tissue mass that adversely affects health; because direct measurement of fat mass is impractical in routine clinical practice, the body mass index (BMI = weight/height² in kg/m²) is used as a proxy (Harrison 22e p.3181).

WHO BMI classes: underweight <18.5; normal 18.5–24.9; overweight 25–29.9; obesity ≥30 kg/m². AACE/ACE management staging further subdivides obesity into class I (30.0–34.9), class II (35.0–39.9), and class III / extreme obesity (≥40) with correspondingly higher disease risk (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187).

BMI-based cutoffs were derived largely from white Western populations; adverse outcomes occur at lower BMI in other ethnic groups, so lower thresholds and ethnic-specific waist-circumference cutpoints (e.g., South Asians/Chinese, Japanese) are recommended (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187).

Fat distribution matters independent of overall BMI: a waist-to-hip ratio >0.9 in women and >1.0 in men, and excess abdominal (visceral) adiposity, are independently associated with type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187).

Energy balance is under homeostatic control by the hypothalamus, which integrates the adipose-derived hormone leptin (rises with fat stores, falls fast with caloric restriction) with gut signals — GLP-1, CCK, GIP, PYY, oxyntomodulin, ghrelin — plus pancreatic insulin and amylin (Harrison 22e p.3181–3182).

Insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia is one of the earliest and most prominent biochemical abnormalities of obesity, is worse with central adiposity, and underlies/precedes many adverse cardiometabolic consequences (Harrison 22e p.3186).

Two leading (not mutually exclusive) hypotheses link obesity to insulin resistance: adipose-tissue inflammation (macrophage accumulation around dying adipocytes), and ectopic lipid deposition once safe adipose storage capacity is exceeded — with stronger human data supporting the ectopic-fat / limited-storage mechanism (Harrison 22e p.3186).

Obesity care begins with sensitive, non-stigmatizing language and an obesity-focused history covering diet, physical activity, sleep, stress, contributing factors, complications, and the patient's readiness/motivation to change (Harrison 22e p.3187–3188).
harrison.pathophysiology: Adipose tissue evolved to store excess calories as triglyceride in unilocular lipid droplets and release free fatty acids and glycerol when needed. In an obesogenic environment (abundant energy-dense palatable food, larger portions, reduced physical activity), chronic energy intake exceeding expenditure — even by as little as ~7 kcal/day sustained over years — produces a cumulative excess of adipose triglyceride. Genetic factors strongly determine individual susceptibility (twin studies show adiposity tracks with biological, not adoptive, family), acting largely through the brain's control of food intake. Body weight is homeostatically defended by the hypothalamus, which integrates the adipose hormone leptin (whose fall below an individual's habitual level is a powerful drive to eat) with gut hormones (GLP-1, CCK, GIP, PYY, oxyntomodulin, ghrelin) and pancreatic insulin/amylin. Within the arcuate nucleus, leptin stimulates POMC neurons (whose products α-/β-MSH act via MC4R in the paraventricular nucleus to reduce intake and raise energy expenditure) and inhibits orexigenic AGRP/NPY/GABA neurons. Leptin defends strongly against fat loss but responds weakly to fat excess ("leptin resistance"), explaining why rising leptin does not prevent obesity. As obesity develops, the earliest abnormality is insulin resistance with compensatory hyperinsulinemia, worse with central fat; this arises from adipose-tissue inflammation and/or ectopic lipid deposition in liver and muscle once safe adipose storage capacity is exceeded (the human data favouring the ectopic-fat mechanism, as illustrated by lipodystrophy). Insulin resistance/hyperinsulinemia then predisposes to the metabolic, endocrine, and cardiovascular complications of obesity (Harrison 22e p.3181–3186).
additionalDifferentials: Hypothyroidism — may cause weight gain but is rarely the sole cause of severe obesity; check TSH (and free thyroxine for rare secondary hypothyroidism) in any patient presenting with obesity (Harrison 22e p.3185, 3188)

Cushing's syndrome / endogenous hypercortisolism — suggested by spontaneous bruising, livid striae, myopathy and marked centripetal fat distribution; confirmed via 24-h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression (Harrison 22e p.3185)

Hypothalamic obesity — from tumors (e.g., craniopharyngioma), inflammatory masses, or severe head injury disrupting hypothalamic energy-balance centres, often with anterior/posterior pituitary dysfunction and short history of hyperphagia (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Insulinoma — weight gain driven by frequent eating to avoid hypoglycemia (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Polycystic ovarian syndrome — secondary cause/association meriting evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3188)

Monogenic / syndromic obesity — leptin or leptin-receptor deficiency, POMC, PCSK1, MC4R, SIM1, BDNF/TrkB, SH2B1 mutations; syndromes such as Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl, Albright's hereditary osteodystrophy/pseudohypoparathyroidism, Cohen's, Carpenter's, Alström's, Tubby (Harrison 22e p.3183–3185)

Drug-induced weight gain — insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, glucocorticoids, antipsychotics (clozapine, olanzapine, risperidone), lithium, antidepressants (tricyclics, MAOIs, paroxetine, mirtazapine), antiepileptics (valproate, gabapentin, carbamazepine) (Harrison 22e p.3188)
nonInfectiousMimics: Very muscular body habitus — BMI may overestimate body fat (Harrison 22e p.3181)
Peripheral edema from NSAIDs or calcium channel blockers — increases weight without increasing body fat (Harrison 22e p.3188)
additionalInvestigations: BMI calculation plus waist circumference (surrogate for visceral fat; measure horizontally above the iliac crest, particularly when BMI ≤35) and/or waist-to-hip ratio (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187)
Fasting lipid profile (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides), chemistry panel, glycated haemoglobin, and blood pressure in all patients (Harrison 22e p.3187)
TSH ± free thyroxine to evaluate for hypothyroidism (Harrison 22e p.3185, 3188)
24-h urinary free cortisol or dexamethasone suppression test when Cushing's syndrome is suspected (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Genetic testing in severe early-onset obesity (up to ~20% of children with severe obesity have chromosomal abnormalities or highly penetrant mutations) (Harrison 22e p.3183)
redFlags: Short history of hyperphagia and rapid weight gain with signs of anterior/posterior pituitary dysfunction — suggests hypothalamic damage from tumor, inflammation, or head injury (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Spontaneous bruising, livid striae, proximal myopathy, marked centripetal fat — suggests Cushing's syndrome rather than common obesity (Harrison 22e p.3185)
Severe early-onset obesity in childhood with intense hyperphagia/food-seeking — prompts screening for monogenic/syndromic causes (Harrison 22e p.3183–3185)
Severe hypertriglyceridemia secondary to insulin resistance — risk of pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.3186)
harrison.prognosis: Obesity is a serious, highly heterogeneous chronic disease that increases morbidity and mortality across many organ systems. The number and severity of complications generally rise with increasing BMI, and excess abdominal/visceral fat confers added cardiometabolic risk. As BMI rises by 5 kg/m², cancer mortality increases by ~10%; in some countries obesity has overtaken smoking as the leading risk factor for cancer. People with obesity have increased morbidity and mortality from atherothrombotic vascular disease (coronary artery disease, stroke) even without diabetes, and are at increased risk of heart failure (especially diastolic dysfunction) and atrial fibrillation. Modest, sustained weight loss (an initial goal of ~8–10% over 6 months) improves obesity-related complications and quality of life; some complications, including type 2 diabetes (e.g., the DiRECT trial showed remission in nearly half of participants with intensive low-energy dietary intervention), can substantially improve or remit with weight loss (Harrison 22e p.3186–3187, 3190).
pitfalls: Treating BMI alone: BMI only reflects body size, not body composition, fat distribution, health, or quality of life — not all patients with a high BMI need treatment, and BMI overestimates fat in very muscular individuals (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187, 3190).

Applying white-Western-derived BMI cutoffs uniformly: adverse outcomes occur at lower BMI in other ethnic groups, and ethnic-specific (e.g., Asia-Pacific) thresholds should be used (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187).
Overlooking that severe hypothyroidism is rarely the sole cause of severe obesity, yet thyroid function should still always be checked (Harrison 22e p.3185).
Mistaking the lower GH response to provocative testing in common obesity for a structural hypothalamic-pituitary lesion (Harrison 22e p.3186).
Assuming a specific macronutrient ratio is key: weight loss depends primarily on total caloric reduction and adherence, not on the proportion of carbohydrate, fat, or protein (Harrison 22e p.3190).

Using stigmatizing language ('obesity', 'morbid obesity', 'fatness') rather than neutral terms ('weight', 'excess weight', 'unhealthy weight'), which leaves patients feeling judged (Harrison 22e p.3188).
Initiating lifestyle change before assessing readiness, which leads to frustration and may hamper future efforts (Harrison 22e p.3188).
harrison.severityClassification: BMI-based (kg/m²): underweight <18.5; healthy/normal weight 18.5–24.9; overweight 25.0–29.9; obesity class I 30.0–34.9 (high disease risk); obesity class II 35.0–39.9 (very high risk); extreme/class III obesity ≥40 (extremely high risk). Risk is refined by excess abdominal fat (ethnic-specific waist-circumference cutpoints; waist-to-hip ratio >0.9 women / >1.0 men). Disease-staging systems augment BMI: the AACE/ACE staging (stage 0 = no complications; stage 1 = mild-moderate complications; stage 2 = at least one severe complication) and the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS, grades 0–4 across medical, functional, and psychological domains, independent of BMI) (Harrison 22e p.3181, 3187–3188).
